subject: mathematics
question_text: By the Gauss-Jordan method, solve x + y + z = 3, 2x + 2y − z = 3, x + y − z = 1.

mark_split.label: Clear column 1 below the leading entry
Write the equivalent system and find z
Introduce a parameter and state the solution set

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.34 — LAQ chapter 3 Matrices, answer 20.3. Printed appearance: TS 17. THIS IS ONE OF ONLY TWO QUESTIONS IN THE WHOLE MATRICES CHAPTER WHOSE ANSWER IS NOT A SINGLE TRIPLE — the other is answer 20.4, which has no solution at all. A student who has practised only the unique-solution questions will try to force x, y and z out of a row of zeros; that is the specific failure this question exists to catch, and it was set in a real TS paper. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S. Book p.34 sets two questions side by side in two columns, leaving no margin for the [N Marks] tags the chapter uses elsewhere. The 1+2+1+2+1 above is deliberately the same shape used for the two unique-solution Gauss-Jordan answers in this unit, so the split does not imply this question is harder than it is; the weight simply moves from clearing upwards (impossible here) to interpreting the zero row. The row-operation chain is the book's own. Star rank is the CHAPTER's ★★★, not this question's. Paper position: Maths-1A Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to the "Introduce a parameter and state the solution set" step.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this by the Gauss-Jordan method — and say what you would do if a whole row turns into zeros.

steps.label: Write the augmented matrix
steps.margin_note: First mark. Nothing about the setup shows that this system is unusual — it is written down exactly like any other. The row of zeros appears two steps later.
steps.memory_tip: Nothing in the setup shows that this system is unusual; the row of zeros appears two steps later.
lines: The system in matrix form is AX = D, where

lines.text: A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \ X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}, \ D = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That the augmented matrix [A | D] is written — the coefficient matrix with the constants column attached.
accept: write the augmented matrix A D with the constants joined to the coefficient matrix
form A given D by putting the right hand side as a fourth column

steps.why: Every row of the augmented matrix is one of the original equations. Holding on to that is what lets you read meaning out of a row of zeros later instead of panicking at it.
common_mistakes: Writing A alone and losing the constants.
Noticing that columns 1 and 2 are identical and stopping; that observation is useful but is not an answer.

steps.label: Clear column 1
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The top-left entry is already 1, so no swap is needed. Subtract multiples of row 1 from the rows below exactly as usual — the method does not change just because the answer will.
steps.memory_tip: The top-left entry is already 1, so no swap. Clear as usual — the method does not change.
lines: Note that column 2 has gone to zero as well.

recall.must_convey: That row 1 is used to clear column 1 below it, and that column 2 goes to zero at the same time.
accept: subtract two times row one from row two and row one from row three to clear the first column
use the leading one to make the first column zero and the second column also becomes zero

steps.why: Columns 1 and 2 of A are identical, so any operation that clears one clears the other. That is the algebraic reason this system cannot pin down x and y separately.
common_mistakes: Treating the zero second column as a mistake and going back to redo the arithmetic.
Applying an operation to part of a row and not to the constant after the rule.

steps.label: Reach the row of zeros
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Rows 2 and 3 are proportional, so one of them cancels completely. A row of all zeros — INCLUDING the constant after the rule — means that equation carried no information, not that something went wrong.
steps.memory_tip: Rows 2 and 3 are proportional, so one cancels completely. A row of all zeros INCLUDING the constant means infinitely many solutions.
lines: The last row is all zeros, so the system has

recall.must_convey: That the third row reduces to all zeros, including the constant, and that this means the system has infinitely many solutions rather than a unique one.
accept: row three becomes all zeros including the constant so the system has infinitely many solutions
the last row vanishes completely which means an infinite solution set
one equation was a repeat so the row goes to zero and there is no unique answer
last row moththam zero avthundi kabatti infinite solutions untai
rows two and three are proportional so one cancels and the solution set is infinite

steps.why: A zero row with a zero constant says 0 = 0, which is true but useless. Two real equations for three unknowns can never fix all three, and that is precisely why the answer has to carry a free letter.
common_mistakes: Confusing this with the no-solution case; there the constant is NOT zero.
Writing 'no solution' when there are in fact infinitely many.
Trying to divide by the zero row to get a pivot.

steps.label: Write the equivalent system
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Turn the surviving rows back into equations. Row 2 fixes z outright; row 1 then ties x and y together but cannot separate them.
steps.memory_tip: Turn the surviving rows back into equations: one fixes z, the other ties x and y together.
lines: The reduced matrix is equivalent to:

recall.must_convey: That the two surviving rows are written back as equations, that row 2 gives z = 1, and that substituting it leaves x + y = 2.
accept: write the rows back as equations, minus three z equals minus three gives z equals one, then x plus y equals two
row two gives z equals one and substituting into row one leaves x plus y equals two
convert the remaining rows to equations and find z is one so x plus y is two
row two nunchi z equals one vasthundi, substitute cheste x plus y equals two
z comes out as one and the first equation then only says x plus y is two

steps.why: z is pinned down but x and y are not — only their SUM is. One equation can never separate two unknowns, and recognising that is the whole answer to this question.
common_mistakes: Trying to find a numerical value for x by guessing.
Dropping the z = 1 result and leaving all three letters free.
Writing x + y = 3 by forgetting to substitute z.

steps.label: Introduce a parameter
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. Name the free unknown with a letter — k is the usual choice — and write everything else in terms of it. Say that k can be any real number; without that the answer is incomplete.
steps.memory_tip: Name the free unknown k and write everything in terms of it. Say that k can be any real number.
lines: Let x = k, where k ∈ R. Then y = 2 − k.

recall.must_convey: That a parameter k is introduced for the free unknown, giving x = k, y = 2 − k, z = 1 with k any real number.
accept: take x equals k where k is any real number then y is two minus k and z is one
put a parameter k for x so the solution set is k, two minus k, one
let x be k then y equals two minus k and z equals one for all real k
x ni k anukunte y equals two minus k, z equals one, k any real number
introduce a parameter and write the solution set in terms of it
reject: x and y can be anything

steps.why: Each value of k gives one genuine solution — k = 0 gives (0, 2, 1) and k = 2 gives (2, 0, 1), and both satisfy all three original equations. The parameter is how you write down infinitely many answers on one line.
common_mistakes: Writing 'infinite solutions' and stopping, with no solution set given.
Forgetting to state that k is a real number.
Giving one particular solution such as (0, 2, 1) as if it were the whole answer.

insider_note: Column 2 goes to zero at the same time as column 1, and that is the tell: the last row becomes all zeros. Infinitely many solutions follow, so introduce a parameter k and write x, y, z in terms of it.
